detail.extracted_title: Beyond the Tanker Contract: Maryam Al Naufali on Turning Asian Energy Demand into Omani Capability
detail.excerpt: As Asian buyers absorb more than ninety percent of Omani crude and domestic grid renewables double in a single year, energy and sustainability researcher Eng. Maryam bint Ahmed Al Naufali argues that lasting economic returns come from the engineering, supply chains, and industrial skills built inside the Sultanate.
detail.article_html:
Across the Arabian Sea, the center of gravity in global energy trade keeps tilting east. China, India, Japan, and South Korea sit at the forefront of world hydrocarbon consumption, and emerging Asian economies are projected to account for a major share of global oil demand growth through 2030. For Oman, whose open-ocean ports face those sea lanes directly, the eastward pull shapes almost every cargo manifest: Central Bank of Oman figures for 2024 show that China alone imported roughly 290.2 million barrels out of Oman’s 308.4 million exported barrels of crude—94.1 percent of the national total.

Yet in an extensive dialogue with Oman Daily journalist Rahma Al Kalbani, energy and sustainability researcher Eng. Maryam bint Ahmed bin Yousuf Al Naufali cautions against mistaking reliable shipment volumes for a finished economic strategy. Political stability, operational track records, and strict contract adherence earn Oman trust among Asian buyers seeking dependable corridors, she notes, while long-term competitiveness rests on turning a supplier relationship into shared industrial production. “Resources can be exported, whereas national capabilities guarantee the continuity of economic returns over the long run,” Al Naufali observes.

Reading Asia’s Shifting Fuel Mix Without Illusions

Any realistic roadmap for Oman’s eastern partnerships has to reckon with two simultaneous trends inside Asian markets: continued near-term reliance on oil and gas alongside accelerating investment in electrification and low-carbon technologies. Global electric vehicle sales surpassed 20 million units in 2025—growing 20 percent in a single year, led by China—and International Energy Agency projections point toward roughly 23 million units by the close of 2026. Over the medium and long term, rapid electrification in road transport will curb gasoline and diesel growth in major Asian cities.

Even so, Al Naufali emphasizes that global oil demand is reshaped gradually rather than overnight. Petrochemical feedstocks, aviation, maritime shipping, and heavy manufacturing lack quick substitutes, keeping hydrocarbons central to Asian industrial security for years to come. Liquefied natural gas markets show a similarly nuanced picture: China’s LNG imports fell by roughly 8.9 million tonnes in 2025 to 69.77 million tonnes amid shifting spot prices, expanding domestic output, pipeline gas inflows, and faster renewable additions, even as South and Southeast Asian buyers continue turning to LNG as a cleaner industrial and power-sector bridge fuel.

Three Yardsticks Beyond Headline MoUs

Because heavy reliance on a single buyer leaves any exporter exposed to shifts in one country’s industrial cycle or energy policy, Al Naufali outlines three practical gauges for evaluating Oman’s Asian partnerships beyond ceremonial announcements and memoranda of understanding.

The first is buyer and market diversification—broadening export destinations across India, Japan, South Korea, and emerging Asian hubs while pairing supply contracts with joint downstream and industrial ventures that anchor mutual long-term stakes. The second is domestic value-added: how deeply Asian-backed projects integrate Omani small and medium enterprises into local supply chains, commission domestic engineering and technical services, transfer industrial know-how, and train Omani specialists.

The third gauge tracks export composition itself. Preliminary data from the National Centre for Statistics and Information through the end of July 2026 show Oman recording a trade surplus of OMR 5.5 billion as total merchandise exports climbed 17.8 percent to OMR 15.9 billion. Oil and gas exports rose 21.6 percent to OMR 10.4 billion over that period, whereas non-oil Omani exports stood at OMR 4.3 billion—clear evidence that hydrocarbons still carry the external balance and that Asian capital must increasingly power manufacturing, logistics, and processing industries capable of expanding non-oil trade.

Doubling Grid Renewables and Grounding Green Hydrogen

Inside the Sultanate, momentum in clean electricity is already creating concrete entry points for Asian technology and capital. Grid-connected renewable sources more than doubled their share of Oman’s total electricity generation in a single year, climbing from 4.26 percent in 2024 to 9.46 percent in 2025 as clean output topped four million megawatt-hours. National targets call for lifting renewables to between 30 and 40 percent of electricity generation by 2030, rising to 60 to 70 percent in 2040 and 90 to 100 percent by 2050.

Reaching those thresholds, Al Naufali notes, requires more than abundant desert sunlight and coastal wind. Investors look closely at transmission grid upgrades, energy storage capacity, operational flexibility, clear regulatory frameworks, and bankable domestic or export demand that can carry projects from planning boards into commercial operation.

That same discipline applies to green hydrogen, one of Oman’s flagship bets for linking clean power to industrial manufacturing and future export corridors. In December 2025, Hydrom announced the mutual conclusion of two earlier project agreements—the BP development and the POSCO–ENGIE consortium—reflecting tougher global financing conditions, evolving off-take markets, and ongoing developer portfolio reviews worldwide. Seven other contracted projects continue advancing toward Oman’s target of producing roughly one million tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2030, though Al Naufali warns against treating earlier portfolio estimates of 1.38 million tonnes as guaranteed output before financing closes, binding off-take contracts are signed, and final investment decisions are reached. Across hydrocarbons, solar arrays, and hydrogen molecules alike, the decisive test remains how much lasting technical capability stays in Omani hands.

Sources

  • Oman Daily
detail.instagram_caption:
China absorbed 290.2 million of Oman's 308.4 million exported crude barrels in 2024—94.1 percent of the national total—while global electric vehicle sales passed 20 million units in 2025. Yet energy and sustainability researcher Eng. Maryam bint Ahmed Al Naufali points out that aviation, shipping, petrochemicals, and heavy manufacturing make Asia's fuel shift gradual, giving Oman a vital window to convert eastern energy ties into domestic industrial capacity.

Rather than counting headline memoranda, Al Naufali proposes judging Asian partnerships by three concrete benchmarks: diversifying buyers across India, Japan, South Korea, and emerging Asian hubs; embedding Omani SMEs, engineers, and technical specialists into local supply chains; and lifting non-oil exports, which stood at OMR 4.3 billion alongside OMR 10.4 billion in oil and gas exports through July 2026.

Clean power inside the Sultanate is already moving fast: grid-connected renewables more than doubled from 4.26 percent of electricity generation in 2024 to 9.46 percent in 2025, exceeding four million megawatt-hours on the path toward 30 to 40 percent by 2030. Meanwhile, seven contracted Hydrom green hydrogen developments continue advancing after two earlier agreements concluded in December 2025, underscoring why grid storage, clear regulation, and final investment decisions separate paper capacity from lasting Omani capability.
